articles.title: When Will We Know the Results of the Midterm Elections?

articles.summary: Election Day is underway, with tens of millions of voters heading to the polls around the U.S. But it could be days, or even weeks, before it becomes clear which party will control each chamber of Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s second term. Some races are likely to be called on Tuesday night, while in other, tighter contests it could take multiple days—if not longer—to determine a winner. It all boils down to the states, which the U.S. Constitution empowers to establish the times, places, and manners of holding elections and counting ballots. Certain states are known for having shorter count times, such as Florida. Others typically take longer, like California, due to its size, and Alaska, where ranked-choice voting can make the process of certifying votes more complicated. “There are all these differences, both in process and deadlines, and geography, and who the voters are, and who the candidates are, that make a difference in what this looks like,” Mitchell Brown, a professor of political science at Auburn University and the author of “How We Vote: Innovations in American Elections,” tells TIME. articles.summary: The midterms are raising fresh questions about the federal government’s role in election security, and where to draw the line between protecting the vote and intervening in the electoral process. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, once a leader in election security, has scaled back its work in President Donald Trump’s second term, raising concerns about the government’s ability to identify and respond to foreign interference. The Justice Department announced its “ largest monitoring effort in history ” today, deploying observers across all 50 states, though a federal judge has ruled that monitors cannot be sworn law enforcement officials or make arrests. The Michigan Attorney General’s Office contacted the DOJ after receiving reports that the department’s monitors were speaking with poll workers in Dearborn and Flint, actions outside the scope of their duties. There are no roads on Everest, meaning that trekkers and guides who give up on the climb or need medical attention sometimes use helicopters for transportation. The man who was killed was identified as 47-year-old Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu, an Indian national, according to local authorities.
